A high-performance SHACL validator

Usage: shacl.exe [OPTIONS] --data <DATA>...

Options:
  -d, --data <DATA>...
          The data graph to validate. A path, an `http(s)` URL, or `-` for standard input.
          
          Repeat it to merge several documents into one graph. Blank nodes stay separate per document, as they must: `_:a` in two files is two nodes.

  -s, --shapes <SHAPES>...
          The shapes graph, on the same terms as `--data` and likewise repeatable. Defaults to the data graph, matching the convention that a self-describing document carries its own shapes.
          
          Only one input in total may be `-`, since standard input can be read only once.

      --data-format <DATA_FORMAT>
          The data graph's RDF syntax. Guessed from the file extension, or over HTTP from the `Content-Type`, when omitted; required when `--data` is `-`, which has neither
          
          [alias: --df]
          [possible values: turtle, n-triples, n-quads, tri-g, rdf-xml, json-ld, n3]

      --shapes-format <SHAPES_FORMAT>
          The shapes graph's RDF syntax, on the same terms as `--data-format`
          
          [alias: --sf]
          [possible values: turtle, n-triples, n-quads, tri-g, rdf-xml, json-ld, n3]

      --build-index
          Cache the parsed data graph beside it as `<file>.shix`, so later runs skip parsing.
          
          Parsing is around three quarters of a run over a large graph, and a data graph that has not changed is parsed identically every time. The cache is checked against the source on every use, so a stale one is never read — see `--no-index`.
          
          Only for a single local `--data` file: a URL has nowhere to write, and merged documents have no one source to check against.

      --no-index
          Ignore any `<file>.shix` cache and parse the data graph

      --threads <N>
          Worker threads for validation. `0` uses every core; `1` runs sequentially.
          
          Only a SHACL Core shapes graph splits across threads. One using `sh:sparql`, a SPARQL-based constraint component or node expressions runs sequentially whatever this says, as does any run with `--max-results`. The report is the same either way, byte for byte.
          
          [default: 0]

  -o, --output <OUTPUT>
          Write the report to a file rather than standard output

      --abort
          Stop at the first result rather than validating the whole graph.
          
          A real early exit, so the report is no longer a complete account of the graph — it answers "is anything wrong" rather than "what is".

      --max-results <N>
          Stop once this many results exist. `--abort` is `--max-results 1`

  -i, --inference <INFERENCE>
          Materialise entailed triples into the data graph before validating.
          
          Off by default: it changes what the report says, since a `sh:closed` shape starts seeing inferred predicates.
          
          [default: none]
          [possible values: none, rdfs]

  -a, --advanced
          Run SHACL-AF rules (`sh:rule`) before validating, so the report sees what they infer.
          
          Spelled as pySHACL spells it. Rules are the one part of SHACL that derives triples rather than reporting on them, which is why they are opt-in: the same data and shapes give a different report with and without this.
          
          [alias: --advanced-mode]

      --iterate-rules <N>
          Apply the rules repeatedly, up to `n` rounds, instead of once.
          
          SHACL-AF defines a single pass and declines to say what repeating it means, so once is the default. But the obvious uses — transitive closure, subclass propagation — need more, and a rule set with no fixpoint stops with an error rather than running forever.
          
          [default: 1]

  -m, --meta-shacl
          Validate the shapes graph itself against SHACL's own shapes first, and refuse to go on if it is malformed
          
          [alias: --metashacl]

  -w, --allow-warnings
          Let `sh:Warning` and `sh:Info` results stand without breaking conformance, as pySHACL's flag of the same name does.
          
          Off by default, because the specification is: `sh:conforms` is false whenever the report holds a result, whatever its severity. The report records the choice as `sh:conformanceDisallows`.
          
          [alias: --allow-warning]

      --allow-infos
          Let `sh:Info` results stand, as pySHACL's flag does
          
          [alias: --allow-info]

  -f, --format <FORMAT>
          How to render the report. `human` is a summary for reading; the rest emit the RDF validation report the SHACL specification defines

          Possible values:
          - human:     One line per result, for reading rather than parsing
          - turtle
          - n-triples
          - rdf-xml
          - json-ld
          
          [default: human]

      --min-severity <MIN_SEVERITY>
          The least severity that breaks conformance. Results below it are still reported, but leave the graph conforming and the exit status 0.
          
          `info` is the default and the specification's: `sh:Info`, `sh:Warning` and `sh:Violation` break conformance, while SHACL 1.2's `sh:Debug` and `sh:Trace` report without blocking. Anything else is recorded in the report as `sh:conformanceDisallows`.

          Possible values:
          - trace:     Every result breaks conformance, `sh:Trace` included
          - debug:     Everything from `sh:Debug` up breaks conformance
          - info:      The specification's default: `sh:Info`, `sh:Warning` and `sh:Violation` break conformance; `sh:Debug` and `sh:Trace` report without blocking
          - warning:   Warnings and violations break conformance
          - violation: Only violations break conformance
          
          [default: info]

  -q, --quiet
          Print only whether the data conforms, not the individual results

      --max-download <BYTES>
          Largest document to accept from a URL, in bytes. A server can stream without end, which no timeout catches
          
          [default: 1073741824]

      --timing
          Report how long loading, compiling and validating each took

      --repeat <REPEAT>
          Validate `n` times, reporting the best wall time. For benchmarking
          
          [default: 1]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version
